faqs.q: Does my East Orange commercial roof replacement require a permit?

runs.v: Yes. A commercial roof replacement requires a construction permit under the New Jersey Uniform Construction Code, because the ordinary-maintenance exemption that waives a permit for a reroof on a detached one- or two-family home does not extend to a commercial, multi-family, or attached building, per N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7. East Orange enforces the code through the East Orange Building Division, with applications filed at the Department of Property Maintenance, East Orange City Hall, 44 City Hall Plaza.

runs.v: A Newark Quality Roofing replacement phases the tear-off and installation in managed sections so the rental units below stay occupied, with each section stripped, insulated, and re-covered before the crew moves on. The staging, debris route, and roof-access plan in the written proposal align with the owner's tenant-notice obligations on multi-family properties, and weekly progress updates keep the property owner informed of the schedule.

faqs.q: Does an East Orange historic building need extra approval for a roof replacement?

runs.v: National Register listing alone places no restriction on a privately funded reroof, per the National Park Service. Local rules can add review, so confirm current requirements with the East Orange Department of Planning, Policy & Development before work begins.

faqs.q: What is the typical lifespan of a new commercial roof?

runs.v: Most commercial membranes need replacement every 15 to 30 years, TPO sometimes sooner: EPDM lasts 15 to 25 years, TPO 7 to 20, modified bitumen 20, built-up roofing 30, and PVC 20 to 30, per the InterNACHI chart and Single Ply Roofing Industry guidance. Standing-seam metal lasts 40 to 80 years, and regular maintenance keeps any system at the long end of its range.

faqs.q: Should you add insulation during a commercial roof replacement?

runs.v: Yes. Commercial roof replacements generally have to meet the energy code, and the tear-off exposes the deck once, the point at which rigid insulation goes in at the lowest added labor. Tapered insulation also builds at least ¼ inch per foot of slope, the drainage that clears ponding water before it stands the 48 hours the NRCA and ARMA count as a defect.
